volumes.title: Lamplighter's Song
volumes.text:
The day goes down behind the mill,
the river keeps the last of it,
and up the lane and down the hill
I come to see the lamps are lit.

One for the baker's shuttered door,
one for the bridge, one for the square,
one for the house where, on the floor,
a child is counting every stair.

I cannot send the dark away.
I only hold it back a pace,
so those still walking home can say
which door is theirs, and know the place.

Good night, you windows, one and all.
My ladder's on my shoulder now.
The small hours come, and they are small
enough to carry, anyhow.

volumes.title: Song for the Last Cup
volumes.text:
The supper things are washed and dried
and stood in rows along the shelf.
One cup is left. I let it bide
and pour the last tea for myself.

The kettle ticks as it grows cold.
The fire mutters to the grate.
Whatever today I was not told
is news tomorrow. It can wait.

Outside, the lamps come on in rows.
Inside, the clock has things to say,
but says them softly, for it knows
I've heard enough of clocks today.

So here's to chairs, and sitting down,
to slippers and a loosened lace,
to being, in a busy town,
one person in one quiet place.

volumes.title: Lullaby for a Wakeful Child
volumes.text:
Hush now. The stairs have gone to bed.
The coats are sleeping on their hooks.
The bread is dreaming it is bread.
The stories doze inside the books.

The moon has put her slippers on
to cross the roofs on quiet rounds.
Your shoes, with all their running gone,
lie on their sides like sleeping hounds.

No, I can't count the stars for you.
There's more of them than there is night.
But I can count from one to two
until you let go of the light.

One. And two. And one. And two.
The blanket's warm. The window's deep.
The whole house holds its breath for you.
Go on ahead. I'll watch you sleep.

volumes.title: The House at Ten
volumes.text:
The house lets down its shoulders now.
The rafters creak like a ship's bow.

The stair that every foot offends
says its one word and makes amends.

The tap lets fall a single drop,
considers, and decides to stop.

The hearth gives back, in ticks and sighs,
the warmth it borrowed. The clock replies.

A mouse behind the skirting board
counts over all it can afford.

And we, who say the house is ours,
are kept by it through the dark hours,

laid safe away, like folded sheets,
in rooms above the emptied streets.

volumes.title: The Cat Goes Out
volumes.text:
At eleven the door opens a crack
and out goes the cat, all whiskers and black,
with nothing to carry, no one to tell,
and a whole town to read by its smell.

Along the wall top, under the lime,
she keeps her appointments and takes her time:
the fishmonger's step, the churchyard gate,
the barrel where something lived of late.

The moon is a saucer. The roofs are a stair.
The kennelled dog pretends she's not there.
She sits on the bridge with her tail in a ring
and listens to nothing, or everything.

Then home, at nobody's command,
to wait on the sill with a look that says: and?
The night was hers. She won't say where.
She sleeps until noon in the warmest chair.

volumes.title: Midnight Song
volumes.text:
Both hands go up. The clock in the square
counts twelve out slowly on the air,
like someone setting twelve plates down
for guests who've long since left the town.

Now it is neither night nor day.
Today has put its coat away.
Tomorrow stands outside the door
and has not been this way before.

The fox stops halfway down the lane.
The weathercock forgets the rain.
For one held breath, from hill to quay,
nothing is owed and all is free.

Then the hands part. The fox moves on.
A minute past, the spell is gone,
and Tuesday, hat in hand, comes in
and looks for somewhere to begin.

volumes.title: For One Who Cannot Sleep
volumes.text:
You've turned the pillow. Turned it twice.
You've counted sheep, who would not stay.
You've given yourself good advice
and listened to it walk away.

So get up. Put the kettle on.
The kitchen, at this hour, is kind.
The lists and letters all are gone
to bed, and left the jam behind.

Sit by the stove. The dark outside
is only the same fields, unlit.
The owl's at work. The tide's the tide.
The world goes on, and you are in it.

And if sleep comes, then let it come
the way a cat comes: when it will.
And if it doesn't, here's a crumb,
a cup, a chair. The night is still.

volumes.title: The Watchman's Round
volumes.text:
Two by the clock, and a clear cold sky.
I walk my round, my lantern and I.

I try the latch of the baker's yard.
I nod to the pump, which is standing guard.

The schoolroom window's open again.
I shut it on tomorrow's rain.

A light upstairs at number nine:
the new baby. All is fine.

A light at the doctor's. A light at the inn,
where somebody's losing who thought he would win.

I know this town by its sleeping sounds,
its snores and its sighs, on my quiet rounds,

and I call the hour, though none of them hear,
so the dark may know that someone is here.

Two by the clock. All's well, all's well.
And what is not well, I do not tell.

volumes.title: The Smallest Hour
volumes.text:
Three is the hour with nothing in it.
The moon's gone down behind the hill.
The clock takes longer for each minute.
Even the river's lying still.

The watchman's gone in to his fire.
The baker has an hour yet.
The owl has all she could desire.
The mouse has what the mouse could get.

Now is the time the old house thinks
of all the feet upon its stair.
Now the well, a long way down, drinks
a star, and keeps it, cold, down there.

If you're awake, you are the one
candle the whole dark is about.
Be easy. It is nearly done.
The night is turning inside out.

volumes.title: The Baker's Song
volumes.text:
I'm up before the birds. I rise,
and so, with luck, will what I make.
I rub the flour from my eyes
and poke the oven fire awake.

Flour and water, salt and yeast,
my two hands and a wooden board.
The window's dark toward the east.
The cat comes in to be ignored.

Push and fold, and fold and press.
The dough grows smooth beneath my thumb.
It's slow work, this, and I confess
I sing to it to make it come.

By five the lane will smell of crust,
and sleepers, turning, half aware,
will dream of breakfast, as they must,
and wake to find it waiting there.

volumes.title: First Bird
volumes.text:
One note, let fall into the dark
the way you'd drop a stone to tell
how deep it is. No answering spark.
A wait. And then one more, as well.

Who sings like that before it's light,
with no proof that the sun will come?
A wren, a scrap of brown, a mite
of faith no bigger than my thumb.

Then others. From the elm, the eaves,
the hedge, the thorn, the orchard wall,
the dark fills up with song like leaves
till there's no room for dark at all.

And in the east, a thread of grey,
as if the singing pulled it through.
The lamps look pale. The night gives way.
The first bird stops. Its work is through.

volumes.title: Morning Song
volumes.text:
The day comes up behind the mill,
the river has the first of it,
and down the lane and up the hill
I put out every lamp I lit.

One by the baker's open door,
where warm bread waits upon the sill.
One by the house where, on the floor,
a child's two shoes are lying still.

The cat is home. The watch is done.
The baker's loaves are on the tray.
The small hours, counted one by one,
add up, as always, to a day.

Good morning, windows, one and all.
I kept the night. It's yours to keep
the day. My ladder's by the wall.
I'm going home. I'm going to sleep.

volumes.title: My Name
volumes.text:
My name is Nell. My name is Sparrow.
A sparrow is a small brown bird.
It is not grand. Its beak is narrow.
It only knows one little word.

The swallow's quick. The hawk is clever.
The cuckoo has a famous song.
The sparrow has no special feather.
But summer birds don't stay for long,

and who is on the windowsill
and in the yard and on the gate?
The sparrow, hopping, cheerful still,
and never early, never late.

So I am glad my name is Sparrow.
I'll have brown feathers and not mind,
and build a nest in the wheelbarrow,
and eat the crumbs you leave behind.

Note: Written by Nell Sparrow at eight, in the back of a sum book.

volumes.title: The School Window
volumes.text:
Miss Pike had set us rivers to say,
the Ember, from the Fells to sea.
I knew them all, until halfway
a sparrow came and looked at me.

She had a straw, and it was long.
She tried the gap beneath the eaves.
She turned it round. Still it went wrong.
She tried it crossways, through the leaves.

She dropped it, fetched it, and not once
did she sit down and say, I can't.
Miss Pike said, "Nell, you dreaming dunce,"
and stood me by the potted plant.

I did not mind. From where I stood
I saw her get it in at last.
I learned the rivers, as I should,
and one thing more, that no one asked.

Note: From Nell Sparrow's school copybook, aged twelve.

volumes.title: Leaving the Fells
volumes.text:
The carrier's cart was at the gate
at six. My box was corded tight.
My mother said, "Now don't be late
for chapel. Write, and write, and write."

My father looked hard at the horse.
The dog ran circles round the wheel.
I said I would come back, of course.
I said it twice, to make it real.

The road went up. I turned to look.
The house was small as a dropped glove.
I had ten shillings and a book
to write in, and my mother's love

packed in among the bread and shoes.
A sparrow rode the tailboard down
past the last gate. And so I chose
to say I had a friend in town.

Note: Nell Sparrow at seventeen, on the road down to Emberwick.

volumes.title: Lodgings in Guildhall Street
volumes.text:
One room. One window. One hard chair.
A jug, a hook, a bed that creaks.
I pay for these, and for the stair,
with all the hats I trim in weeks.

By day I sew on wax and wire,
cherries no bird would ever take.
By night I have a candle's fire,
a pencil, and I stay awake.

Nobody knows me in this town.
Some evenings that is hard to bear,
and some it is a brand-new gown
that only I know how to wear.

The sparrows found my sill today.
Town sparrows, sooty, bold as brass.
They looked at me as if to say:
so you're a Sparrow. So. You'll pass.

Note: Written at twenty, in a room above the hat shop.

volumes.title: The Held Hand
volumes.text:
We walked back from the fair by way
of the river path, which takes too long.
He had not very much to say.
He whistled half of a slow song.

He is a joiner. Will's his name.
He told me how a joint is made.
I said that hats were much the same.
They're not. He nodded, and we stayed

a minute on the bridge. Below,
the water carried off the light.
And then, I don't know how, although
I know which hands, his left, my right,

were holding. Nothing else at all.
A sparrow in the alder scolded.
I've trimmed a hundred hats this fall
and not one thing so neatly folded.

Note: Nell Sparrow at twenty-three. She married the joiner.

volumes.title: Two Chairs
volumes.text:
He made the table and two chairs.
I made the curtains and the bread.
We have two rooms, a flight of stairs,
a kettle, and a lot ahead.

His shavings curl along the floor.
My pins turn up inside his boots.
There's sawdust in the sugar drawer,
and neither of us much disputes

whose house it is. It's ours. It's small.
The sparrows had the eaves before
we came, and pay no rent at all,
and we have let them stay. What's more,

I think that they have let us stay.
They watch us through the windowpane
at supper, in a landlord's way,
then tuck their heads in from the rain.

Note: Written in the first winter of her marriage.

volumes.title: Cradle Song
volumes.text:
Small fist. Small yawn. Small furious face.
You came in on a night of rain
and took up every inch of space,
and none of it is ours again.

Your father pegged your cradle, oak,
without a nail, and rubbed it smooth.
I stitched a quilt. Neither one spoke
of being frightened. That's the truth.

I used to count my lines at night,
five beats, or four, and cross them through.
Now I count breaths, by candlelight,
and every single one is you.

Sleep, little sparrow, small and brown.
The eaves are full of sleeping kin.
The rain is walking through the town.
The door is shut, and you are in.

Note: For her daughter Wren, born that spring.

volumes.title: Washing Day
volumes.text:
Four shirts, two sheets, six pinafores.
The copper's lit. The yard is steam.
A poem tried both kitchen doors
this morning, and it would not seem

to hear me say: when they're asleep.
It is not that kind of a guest.
So here it is, upon a heap
of washing list, and second-best.

Three children and a husband's sleeves.
Soap, blue-bag, starch, a line, some pegs.
The sparrows queue along the eaves
and comment on the stockings' legs.

I'm thirty-eight. My hands are red.
My verses used to scan and shine.
Now they are shirts, and they are bread.
I hang them, flapping, on the line.

Note: Found on the back of a laundry list.

volumes.title: The Empty Stair
volumes.text:
The youngest left today. Her box
went bumping down the stairs at eight.
The house is very full of clocks.
I had not noticed that, of late.

I laid five places. Took back three.
Will looked at them and looked away.
He said the gate wants oil. To me
that meant what he could not quite say.

I told my mother I would write.
I did, some weeks. I know now what
she did with every other night:
she watched the lane, and said she'd not.

The sparrows' second brood has flown.
The old birds sit along the wall,
a little ruffled, on their own,
not minding, or not much, at all.

Note: Written the day her youngest left for the coast.

volumes.title: His Bench
volumes.text:
His plane lies where he set it down.
The shavings by the vice are dry.
I sweep the rest of the house, and frown,
and leave this room, and don't ask why.

He made the table, forty years
ago, both chairs, the cradle, and
the door that never sticks. One hears
a man in what he made by hand.

There's more of him in every joint
than in the likeness on the wall.
His chair still holds me. That's the point
of making things well, after all.

The sparrows come at four for bread.
He fed them. Now they come to me.
I tell them things he would have said.
They tip their heads. They let me be.

Note: Written the winter after Will died.

volumes.title: Old Sparrow
volumes.text:
I'm smaller than I used to be.
The top shelf is a foreign land.
The stairs and I do not agree.
My knitting has got out of hand.

The children in the lane call me
Old Sparrow, when they think I'm deaf.
I'm not. I like it. Let it be.
It's what I was at eight, myself.

I wear brown wool. I hop a bit.
I keep an eye on every gate.
I have a sunny place to sit,
and am not early, am not late.

Wren's grandchild, who is nearly four,
asked what a poem's for. I said:
it's something left outside the door
for anyone who wants some bread.

Note: Nell Sparrow at eighty, still in the joiner's house.

volumes.title: Crumbs on the Sill
volumes.text:
I've put the crumbs out on the sill.
I've banked the fire and wound the clock.
The lane is white. The eaves are still.
I have not turned the kitchen lock.

I wrote my verses on the backs
of sum books, bills and washing lists.
A life gets in between the cracks
of other things, and so persists.

I had a name that suited me.
I had two chairs, a hand to hold,
a cradle, and a window. See
how much that is, now that it's told.

If you have found this, then you came
as sparrows do, for what was spread.
Take what you like. I'd do the same.
That's all. It's time I went to bed.

Note: Her last poem, written at eighty-four.

volumes.title: First Frost
volumes.text:
This morning the grass
had been written on.
Every blade signed
in a white, careful hand.

The water butt wore a lid
thin as a watch glass.
I broke it with one finger
and felt like a thief.

The last three apples
hung on in the top of the tree,
each with a cap of rime.
The robin had opinions.

So it begins.
I went in and found my gloves,
one in each pocket
of last winter's coat,
still holding the shape of my hands.

volumes.title: The Elm Lets Go
volumes.text:
All October the elm
gave its leaves away
like a shopkeeper closing down:
handfuls, armfuls, everything must go.

Now it stands in its bones.
You can see what it was hiding:
three old nests,
a kite from some other summer,
the whole sky.

The wind goes through
and finds nothing to argue with.

I used to think bare trees were sad.
Today I think
they are only resting their arms,
having carried green
since April without once putting it down.

volumes.title: The Woodpile
volumes.text:
Ash for a quick fire,
oak for a long one,
apple for the smell,
and none of it green.

We stack it under the eaves
bark side up, the way my father did,
each log a small roof
for the log beneath.

By dusk there is a wall
between us and January,
chest-high and smelling of sap.
The wren has already moved in.

A woodpile is a kind of sum.
So many cold nights,
so many armfuls,
and something left over for March.

volumes.title: First Snow
volumes.text:
It came in the night
without knocking.

By morning it had finished
the garden wall,
rounded the pump,
and given the scarecrow
a clean white shirt.

No cart had passed.
The lane lay like a page
nobody had the heart to begin.

Then a cat began it,
small neat commas
from the hedge to the dairy door.
Then the milk boy.
Then, shrieking, every child in Emberwick
with a tea tray under one arm.

volumes.title: The Shortest Day
volumes.text:
Today the sun
got up late, did little,
and left before four,
like a guest who has another party.

We lit the lamps at three.
The hens went to roost
thinking a week had passed.
Shadows lay down full length
across the frozen field
and did not get up.

Still. This is the turn.
From tonight the dark
gives back a minute, then two,
shy as someone returning
a thing they borrowed in June.
I will count each one.

volumes.title: The Midwinter Table
volumes.text:
Every chair we own,
and the piano stool,
and a box with a cushion on it.

The goose has gone round twice.
There are nuts in a blue bowl,
a pudding dark as a wet road,
candles in the windows
so the lane can see us.

Grandfather is asleep
with a paper crown over one eye.
The children are under the table
running a country of their own.

Outside it is the deep middle of the cold.
In here somebody starts a song,
gets the second verse wrong,
and all of us follow, gladly, into the mistake.

volumes.title: New Year on the Bridge
volumes.text:
At midnight we walk down to the bridge
because we always have.

The Ember goes under, black and quick,
carrying off the old year
in pieces of broken moon.

Someone has brought a bell.
Someone has brought a flask.
The clock in the square strikes,
and for twelve strokes nobody says anything.

Then everyone says it at once,
and shakes hands with gloves on,
which hardly counts,
so we take them off and do it again.

The first thing I do this year
is get cold fingers
in excellent company.

volumes.title: Ice on the Millpond
volumes.text:
Three days of iron frost
and the miller walks out
to the middle, jumps twice,
and waves his hat.

By noon the pond is a fairground.
Boys on barrel staves.
The doctor, astonishingly graceful,
hands behind his back.
The schoolmistress going backwards
faster than is quite proper.

I have one borrowed skate
and no talent.
I go round the edge
holding the willows by the hand,
and under my feet, through grey glass,
a slow gold carp looks up at all of us.

volumes.title: Snowed In
volumes.text:
The door opens inward, luckily.
Behind it stands a second door,
white, with the latch printed in it backwards.

No post. No bell. No road.
The world has shrunk
to a kitchen, a fire, a cat,
a shelf of jars we filled in August
without knowing it was for today.

We play draughts with buttons.
We read the almanac aloud.
We bake, because the oven is the warmest thing we know.

At dusk I scrape a hole in the window frost
the size of one eye.
Blue snow. One star.
The pump wearing a tall white hat,
and nothing, anywhere, expecting me.

volumes.title: The Long Month
volumes.text:
Nobody writes verses about this part.
The feast is eaten.
The snow has gone grey at the edges
like a tired tablecloth.

My boots have not been dry since Tuesday.
The woodpile is down to its knees.
The hens are sulking.
The sky comes down each morning
as far as the chimney and stays.

So I mend.
A sock, a strap, the hinge on the gate,
a quarrel with my neighbour over the ditch.

It is not much.
But winter is long in the middle,
and you get across it
the way you cross a ploughed field:
by the next furrow, and the next.

volumes.title: Snowdrops Under the Hedge
volumes.text:
I was not looking for them.
I was looking for the other glove.

Under the hedge, where the drift
had pulled back an inch,
there they were:
five, six, a dozen,
heads down, like children
who have come to the party early
and are too shy to knock.

Green on white. White on white.
Each one no taller than a thimble
and entirely unafraid of February.

I did not pick them.
I went and fetched everyone in the house,
and we stood in the cold
and were, all of us, extremely pleased.

volumes.title: The Thaw
volumes.text:
It begins as a sound.
One drop from the eaves,
then another, counting.

By noon every gutter in Emberwick
is telling the same long story.
The lane runs brown.
The pump takes off its hat.
The scarecrow gets his old coat back.

On the Ember the ice goes out
with a groan like a great door,
and the river, which was only waiting,
shoulders through.

I hang my gloves on the nail by the door,
one over the other,
still holding the shape of my hands.
Somewhere a blackbird
tries the first two notes of spring, and keeps them.

volumes.title: Ode to the Door Key
volumes.text:
O small brass tooth,
warm from my pocket,
who has travelled all day
among pennies and string
and never once complained.

You know one thing,
and you know it perfectly.
Of all the doors in Emberwick
there is a single lock
that turns for you
like a head at its own name.

I have lost you in every coat I own.
I have found you each time
in the last place, naturally.

Now do your one trick.
There. The click,
the give, the smell of home
coming out to meet me in the hall.

volumes.title: Ode to the Doormat
volumes.text:
You get the worst of us.
The marsh, the lane, the farmyard,
whatever the dog has found
and thought worth bringing home.

Nobody thanks a doormat.
We arrive, we scuff, we go in
to be greeted by better furniture.

Yet you are the house's first word,
and the word is: stop.
Leave the weather outside.
Leave the long road.
Leave whatever happened at the market.

Bristly, patient, flat as Tuesday,
you lie across the threshold
like an old dog who has decided
that this, exactly this, is his work.
I wipe my feet twice today, out of respect.

volumes.title: Ode to the Kettle
volumes.text:
Round-bellied, black-bottomed,
dented where somebody dropped you
in the year of the flood,
you sit on the hob like a small judge.

Other pots are for occasions.
You are for everything:
bad news, good news, wet feet,
visitors, no visitors,
four in the afternoon.

I love how you begin,
a tick, a mutter,
a rumour of weather inside you,
then the long rising note
that means: sit down,
it will all look different in a minute.

And it does.
You have never once been wrong.

volumes.title: Ode to the Wooden Spoon
volumes.text:
You were pale once, and straight.
Now you are the colour of gravy
and lean a little to the left,
worn to the shape
of forty years of stirring.

You have been in every soup,
every porridge, every jam,
the custard that curdled,
the famous Harvest Supper gravy.
You have been a drumstick,
a pointer, a sceptre,
and once, briefly, a boat.

There are silver spoons in the drawer.
They come out at weddings
and lie about looking handsome.

But when the pot is hot
and the moment matters,
the hand goes to you
without asking the head.

volumes.title: Ode to the Kitchen Table
volumes.text:
Four legs, one of them short,
and a folded paper under it
that has outlasted two mayors.

On your back we have rolled pastry,
done sums, shelled peas,
signed papers, cut out a wedding dress,
and bathed a baby in a tin basin.

You are scarred like an old sailor.
Here, a ring from a hot pan.
Here, the initials of a boy
who is now a grandfather
and still denies it.

Every table is an altar of sorts.
Ours asks for nothing
but elbows, crumbs and news,
and that whoever comes in cold
should sit down first and explain afterwards.

volumes.title: Ode to the Stairs
volumes.text:
Thirteen of you,
and I could climb you asleep,
and have.

The third from the bottom complains.
It has complained since before I was born.
Every child of this house
learned to step over it,
coming in late,
and every parent, lying awake,
learned to listen for the step that was missed.

You are worn in the middle
like old doorsteps.
We have carried up you
candles, coal, trays, cradles,
one piano, never again,
and each other.

Going up is the day ending.
Coming down is the day begun.
In between, good stairs, you hold your breath.

volumes.title: Ode to the Landing Window
volumes.text:
You are the house's eye,
and you do not blink.

Through you I have checked the weather
ten thousand mornings
and been wrong about it most.

You frame the same things daily:
the pear tree, the wall,
a strip of the Ember, the far Fells.
Yet you have never shown me
the same picture twice.

Rain writes on you.
Frost draws ferns.
Flies consult you at length
about the way out.

And at night, when the lamp is lit,
you turn politely into a mirror,
and show the house to itself:
a stair, a light, a face going up to bed.

volumes.title: Ode to the Armchair
volumes.text:
You have my shape by now.
Anyone else who sits in you
feels like a guest in someone's coat.

Your arms are worn to the weave.
One spring has ideas of its own.
Down your sides, I am certain,
live a thimble, three pencils,
a sixpence, and the spectacles
I accused the cat of taking.

In you I have read whole winters.
In you I have slept through the endings
of a hundred books.

Thrones are for sitting up straight.
You are for the other thing:
the long outward breath,
the boots off,
the book open face down on one knee
while the fire does the thinking.

volumes.title: Ode to the Lamp
volumes.text:
All day you are nothing much.
A glass chimney, a brass belly,
a wick like a tired shoelace.

Then four o'clock comes down the lane
and I strike a match,
and you open your one gold eye.

At once the room has a middle.
The corners step back.
The table gathers its cloth about it.
Faces lean in, and are kinder
than they looked by day.

You smoke when I neglect you.
You sulk in a draught.
You want trimming, filling, polishing,
like any small household god.

But a page read by your light
stays read.
And a window with you in it
is how a traveller knows a house from a hill.

volumes.title: Ode to a Bar of Soap
volumes.text:
Yellow, square-shouldered,
smelling of nothing but clean,
you came into this house
the size of a brick.

Look at you now.
A sliver, a wafer, a new moon
in a saucer by the basin.

You are the only thing I know
that does its work
by disappearing.
Every pair of hands takes a little.
The gardener's, the baker's,
the child's who only pretended.

You have washed off the whole day,
ink, earth, onions, the argument,
and asked no questions.

Tomorrow I shall press what is left of you
onto the back of the next bar,
and you will go on, as the good do, unnoticed.

volumes.title: Ode to the Blanket
volumes.text:
Grey wool, blue stripe,
a darn in one corner
shaped like the island of somewhere.

You were my grandmother's.
You have been a tent,
a cloak, a sail, a stage curtain,
and a river for tin boats to cross.
You have been wrapped round fevers
and carried to picnics
and hung out every April
to be beaten like a carpet and forgiven.

Tonight you are only a blanket,
which is the best thing you do.

Weight without heaviness.
Warmth that asks nothing back.
I pull you up to my chin,
and the day, which was large,
folds itself to the size of a bed.

volumes.title: Ode to the Last Candle
volumes.text:
Everything else is done.
The key is on its nail.
The kettle is cold, the spoon is dry,
the table is cleared of all but tomorrow.
The stairs have said their one word.

Now there is you,
a thumb of wax in a tin saucer,
holding up a flame
no bigger than a seed.

By you I can see the whole of my life:
one room,
one window with the dark in it,
one blanket turned down.

Thank you, small light.
Thank you, ordinary things,
that stood where I left you all day long.

I lean close. One breath.
The house keeps the rest.
